sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of an incomplete upper jaw bone measuring 15.6 centimeters in length.
Although the front and top edges are broken, scientists estimate the complete bone would have reached between 19 and 20 centimeters.
This bone preserves twenty-three sockets where teeth once fit.
Ajnabia is the first definitive duck-billed dinosaur found in Africa, challenging the idea that these animals could not cross the ocean to reach the continent.
Its name means stranger or traveler, honoring the Greek hero Odysseus who sailed far from home.
Fossils were recovered from Late Maastrichtian rock layers in phosphate mines located in the Khouribga Province of Morocco.
The rock environment was a near-shore marine setting inhabited by sharks, fish, mosasaurs, and other sea reptiles.
This animal was small, reaching a total length of about 3 meters.
Analysis of the teeth and jaw structure shows it belonged to the Lambeosaurinae subfamily, known for duck-like bills and elaborate head crests.
Researchers suggest that Lambeosaurinae reached North Africa through oceanic dispersal, where adults likely swam or floated between Europe and the continent.
While rafting on floating debris is unlikely for large adults, young hadrosaurs might have been transported this way.
Ajnabia is classified within the family Hadrosauridae and the broader group Ornithischia.
Phylogenetic studies place it in the tribe Arenysaurini, a clade previously known only in Europe.
A 2021 analysis identified it as the sister taxon to Blasisaurus from Spain, while a 2022 study placed it with Pararhabdodon in the Tsintaosaurini.
The species existed from 72.2 to 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage.
It is debated whether intermittent land connections could have served as a dispersal route, though oceanic travel remains the favored explanation.
